title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
hook: the old man who could choose the hour of his death waits for the sun to turn, then asks Krishna for leave to go
carry: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Shanti and Anushasana, Gautami told the hunter to let the snake go, and the chain of blame ran back through Death and Time. Did you find one more link? Today, the teacher's last lesson. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

Bhishma carries an unusual gift. Long ago, his father blessed him so that death would come to him only when he chose it. So he has been lying on the arrows, teaching, and waiting. He's waiting for a particular turning of the year: the time when the sun begins its northward course, called uttarayana, which the tradition holds as an auspicious time to die. Bhishma sent Yudhishthira back to the city to rule. Now the season has turned, and Yudhishthira comes back to the field, with fire and garlands and everything needed for the last rites. Today, how Bhishma goes.
screen: `DEATH ONLY WHEN HE CHOOSES.` → `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO TURN.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Bhishma opens his eyes and sees them all around him: Yudhishthira and his brothers, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Krishna. He says the time has come. He speaks a few last words to Dhritarashtra, the blind king, whose sons are gone, and tells him not to grieve, and to treat the Pandavas as his own. Then he turns to Krishna and asks for leave to go. Notice that. A man who can choose his own death still asks permission to take it. Krishna gives it. And then Bhishma does something the text describes almost like a meditation. He draws his life breath inward, part by part. As it withdraws from each limb, the story says, the arrows in that part of his body fall away and the wound closes. Limb by limb, the bed of arrows lets him go. At last the breath leaves through the crown of his head, rising like a great light into the sky. His family builds the pyre and performs the rites. Then they go down to the Ganga to offer water, and the river goddess herself rises out of it, weeping. Bhishma was her son. She grieves that he fell to Shikhandi. And Krishna comforts her: it was Arjuna who brought him down, he says, with Shikhandi only standing in front, and her son has gone to the heavens. Don't grieve. So the teaching from the bed of arrows ends without a speech: a man finishing his work, asking leave, and going when it's time, while the arrows fall from him one by one.
screen: `"THE TIME HAS COME"` · `HE ASKS KRISHNA FOR LEAVE` · `THE ARROWS FALL AWAY` · then, large: `GANGA WEEPS FOR HER SON`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your body be heavy and supported. Breathe in slowly, and as you breathe out, let one part of your body soften and let go: your feet, then your legs, then your belly, your shoulders, your face. Take your time, part by part, the way the arrows fell away. There's nothing to finish right now. If you pray, you can rest in your prayer as you let go. The bell holds the time.
Shanti and Anushasana. Peace and instruction, ending with Bhishma asking leave, letting go, and the arrows falling from him one by one.
Your line: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows. Today, finish one thing properly, and let it go. Tomorrow, a new book opens: Ashvamedhika. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Bhishma's death at uttarayana is remembered in Hindu tradition, and some communities observe a day in his memory, Bhishma Ashtami, with water offerings in his name.

fork.setup: you're Bhishma. the sun has turned, your family has gathered, and you can choose this moment to die. what do you do first?
options: leave at once, without a word.
speak to Dhritarashtra, then ask Krishna for leave.
wait a little longer to finish teaching.
fork.reveal: he counsels Dhritarashtra not to grieve, then asks Krishna's leave, and withdraws his breath limb by limb.

original.note: the northward course of the sun: the season Bhishma waited for.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bhishma died of his wounds on the field.
what it means: he chose his hour, asked leave of Krishna, and withdrew his breath limb by limb.
what a scholar hears: the death is told as a yogic withdrawal, and the arrows falling away turn the bed of arrows into a release.

notes: All paraphrase. The text gives the number of nights Bhishma lay on the arrows; left out under the claims rule.
Confirm in Ganguli: the description of the breath withdrawing limb by limb with the arrows falling away and wounds healing, and the breath leaving through the crown of the head like a great light.
Confirm Ganga's lament and Krishna's consolation (that Arjuna, not Shikhandi, slew him).
'Tradition holds uttarayana as an auspicious time to die' is attributed to the tradition; confirm.
howItsDone names Bhishma Ashtami as observed by 'some communities' with water offerings; confirm.

Editor: corrected 'gone back to be crowned' (the coronation comes before the visit to Bhishma in Ganguli; Bhishma sends him back to the city); pyre line simplified; the closing uplift ('a lesson no words could give') replaced with a concrete ending.
Audit: ambiguous 'he comes back' (read as Bhishma) clarified to Yudhishthira.
